extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimenters, and telegraph/telephone engineers interested in producing and reproducing sound by light (photophone)
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental guidance and criteria for producing and reproducing sound by means of light (the photophone): selection and preparation of materials (especially selenium), apparatus designs to modulate light, receiver/telephonic detection considerations, and observations about which radiations and diaphragms are effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selenium as a light-sensitive conductor
rubrics_metrics.description: Selenium exhibits changes in electrical resistance when exposed to light; certain allotropic forms conduct at ordinary temperatures while others do not. Exposure to sunlight hastens change of selenium from one allotropic form to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical observations: vitreous (rapidly cooled) selenium is a non-conductor and appears dark-brown; slowly cooled (crystalline/metallic) selenium is a conductor. Willoughby Smith, Sale, Draper, Moss, Adams, Lord Rosse and others verified light sensitivity. Note that different forms have very different resistances and that light (including portions of the spectrum) can markedly reduce resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce an 'undulatory' beam rather than mere intermittence
rubrics_metrics.description: An undulatory beam is a beam that shines continuously upon the receiver but whose intensity is subject to rapid changes corresponding to vibratory movement of air during sound transmission; this is distinct from a merely intermittent beam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reproduce speech the intensity variations of the light on the selenium receiver should graphically resemble the air-vibration curve of the voice. Intermittent (on/off) interruption alone is insufficient for faithful speech reproduction; rapid continuous variations (undulatory) matching voice waveform are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a detector sensitive to rapid changes (telephone analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The telephone (receiver) responds to changes in current, analogous to electric induction: no effect from steady current, audible effect proportional to amount of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the telephone responds to changes, the light-induced variations in selenium conductivity must be rapidly varying. Design the optical modulation so that changes in resistance produce corresponding transient currents to which the telephone is sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulate light at audio frequencies (rapid interruption/variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermit the light with great rapidity so as to produce a succession of changes in the conductivity of the selenium corresponding in frequency to musical vibrations within hearing limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid interruption (higher pitch → more audible). Rotating perforated disks, sliding perforated plates driven by a diaphragm, or other mechanical modulators can produce the required modulation. For loudest effects, rapidly interrupting the beam by a perforated disk was effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus: perforated plates / sliding plates driven by diaphragm
rubrics_metrics.description: Pass light through many small orifices (preferably slits); use two similarly perforated plates, one fixed and one movable attached to the center of a diaphragm actuated by the voice so their relative sliding varies the open area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement allows the diaphragm vibration to alternately enlarge and contract free orifices without completely obstructing light, producing an undulatory beam whose intensity corresponds to voice variations. Place apparatus in path of a parallel beam and focus at receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus: rotating perforated disk (silent rotation advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapidly rotating perforated disk can intermittently interrupt a beam to produce musical tones; silent rotation is advantageous in lab experiments because it doesn't mask receiver audibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an opaque screen near the rotating disk to fully cut the beam by a slight motion of the hand to produce Morse-like dots and dashes. Rotating disk form produces loud effects when rapidly interrupting the beam and is convenient for experimental signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus: flexible mirror attached to diaphragm (best simple form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane mirror of flexible material (silvered mica or microscope glass) with the speaker's voice directed against its back; light reflected from this mirror is thrown into vibrations corresponding to the diaphragm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With concentrated parallel beam and appropriate lenses this simple mirror-transmitter effectively converts voice vibrations into corresponding light modulations for transmission to a distant selenium receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light source and beam conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Any powerful source of light may be used; sunlight was chiefly experimented with. Concentrate a large beam by lens onto transmitting diaphragm-mirror and re-render parallel by another lens. Oxyhydrogen and kerosene lamp light can reproduce articulate speech in laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long distance use, render beam parallel (collimated) and use lenses to concentrate and re-parallelize. Choice of light source affects achievable distance and loudness; stronger sources increase effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver optics and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Receive the beam at a distant station upon a parabolic reflector; place a sensitive selenium-cell in the focus connected in local circuit with battery and telephone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate incoming beam onto selenium cell; experiments demonstrated speech reproduction between points at least 213 metres apart. Use lenses/parabolic reflectors to maximize illumination of the selenium cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce selenium-cell resistance to manageable limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior experiments used selenium-cells with resistances in millions of ohms; practical photophonic receivers require far lower resistances (authors achieved ~300 ohms in the dark, 155 in light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical and chemical cell construction methods (choice of contact metal, annealing procedure) can dramatically lower resistance. Aim for cell resistances low enough to produce detectable telephone currents when illuminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of brass (or chemically interactive metal) for selenium contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Brass, though chemically acted upon by selenium, forms an excellent and convenient material for selenium-cell conductors; chemical action may promote intimate bonding and lower contact resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found brass preferable to platinum in producing low-resistance contacts; metals not chemically acted upon by selenium may give higher contact resistance because melted selenium behaves like water on greasy surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of applying selenium to cell and annealing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat the cell and rub a stick of selenium over the hot surface; then anneal by heating over a gas-stove until surface cloudiness appears (crystallization), continue heating until signs of melting appear then remove heat and cool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper annealing produces crystalline selenium that is conductive and light-sensitive. Heating until crystallization and stopping at first signs of melting yields best results; over-heating that fully melts is detrimental. The operation occupies only a few minutes and produces distinct microscopic crystal structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative beam-modulation methods (polarization, variable-focus lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beam may be polarized and affected by electrical/magnetic influences (Faraday/Kerr effects) or passed through a lens of variable focus to vary intensity on receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polarization methods or variable focus lenses (e.g., lens of Cusco) are viable alternate modulators; choose modulation method suitable to experimental aims and available apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of operative rays — not solely heat-rays
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments with absorbers show that alum or bisulphide of carbon only slightly diminish audible effect, while iodine in bisulphide cuts off most but not all effect; apparently opaque hard rubber sheet did not fully eliminate the effect, suggesting rays involved are not just heat-rays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only thermal radiation is responsible; experiments imply invisible radiations within ordinary beams contribute. Further experiments needed before definitive identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials for producing audible molecular or diaphragm vibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin diaphragms of many substances emit sounds when acted on by an intermittent beam of light: hard rubber and antimony produce loud sounds; paper and mica produce weak sounds; most tested materials (gold, silver, platinum, iron, brass, gutta-percha, hard rubber, paper, wood, mica, silvered glass) yielded measurable effects except carbon and thin glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For experiments in direct optical-to-acoustic conversion (without telephone), choose materials like hard rubber or antimony for stronger audible effects; arrange as diaphragm and listen via hearing-tube to intensify. The effect varies with material stiffness and molecular response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct acoustic detection via illuminated diaphragms
rubrics_metrics.description: Molecular disturbance in crystalline selenium or in diaphragms exposed to intermittent light can be heard directly by placing the ear in close contact or using a hearing-tube; hard-rubber sheet in contact with ear produced distinct musical notes when focused by lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect direct sound without electrical circuit, press a thin diaphragm (hard rubber, etc.) close to the ear or couple with a hearing-tube; focusing an intermittent beam on the diaphragm intensifies effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of opaque screen for signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing an opaque screen near a rotating disk allows full beam-cutting by a slight hand motion, enabling production of Morse-like dots and dashes at the distant receiving station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for remote on/off signaling; combine with silent rotating disk to effect noise-free laboratory tests and distant telegraphy by light interruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impure solvents when regenerating caoutchouc (rubber guidance present earlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caoutchouc may be ruined by the use of impure solvents; when regenerating by evaporation of solvent, take utmost care not to use any solvents which contain fatty or greasy matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing clear solutions for coatings, use Payen's solvent (carbon disulphide mixed with 5% absolute alcohol) at ratios like 1:30 (masticated caoutchouc to solvent) to obtain filterable solutions for delicate moulds. Use alcohol for coagulating small-scale; alum on industrial scale; strain milk and press/dry clot carefully to avoid viscous degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical sensitivities and treatment effects on caoutchouc
rubrics_metrics.description: Different reagents affect caoutchouc differently: weak/dilute acids little effect; strong sulphuric slowly acts and more rapidly with heat; strong nitric causes entire destruction; prolonged action of chlorine, bromine, iodine can destroy though controlled action can vulcanize/strengthen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In processing rubber, control reagent strength and exposure to avoid destruction; coagulation and proper drying prevent conversion of fibrous to viscous constituents which impair properties.
